title: Their defence: evil comes by God's decree but not his efficiency; the creature fails; the entity of the act is good
source_text: XXVIII. Nec tamen inde sequi putant Deum esse peccati autorem: quoniam licet malum Deo decernente fiat, nihilominus non fit Deo efficiente, sed creatura ex certa permissione Dei deficiente. Ac quamvis quod in actione mala positivum est ad Deum ut ad causam efficientem referatur, non tamen propterea Deus mali causa est, quia nempe actionis quantumvis malae entitas est bona, malitia vero formaliter in quadam rectitudinis privatione consistit.
pass_a_gloss: XXVIII. Yet they do not think it follows thence that God is the author of sin: since although evil is done with God decreeing, nevertheless it is not done with God effecting, but with the creature failing from the certain permission of God. And although what is positive in an evil action is referred to God as to the efficient cause, yet God is not on that account the cause of evil, because namely the entity of an action however evil is good, but malice formally consists in a certain privation of rectitude.
pass_b_english: They deny, however, that this makes God the author of sin. Evil happens as God has decreed, yet God is not the one who works it: it comes from the creature falling short, under a definite permission of God.

And although what is positive in an evil action is traced to God as its efficient cause, God is not for that reason the cause of evil. The being of an action, however evil, is good, whereas malice formally consists in a certain lack of rectitude.
